stem: A monochromatic ray of light strike the water \( (n = 4/3) \) surface in a cylindrical vessel at angle of incidence \( 53^{0} \). Depth of water is 36 cm. After striking the water surface, how long will the light take to reach the bottom of the vessel? [Angles of the most popular Pythagorean triangle of sides in the ratio 3:4:5 are nearly \( 37^{0} \), \( 53^{0} \) and \( 90^{0} \)]
our_solution:
**Given:** \( i = 53^\circ \), \( n_{water} = \dfrac{4}{3} \), depth of water \( = 36\ \text{cm} \). Using the stem's own approximation, the 3:4:5 triangle has angles \( 37^\circ \), \( 53^\circ \), \( 90^\circ \), so \( \sin 53^\circ = \dfrac{4}{5} \), \( \sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5} \), \( \cos 37^\circ = \dfrac{4}{5} \).

**Angle of refraction.** By Snell's law,
\( \sin r = \dfrac{\sin i}{n} = \dfrac{4/5}{4/3} = \dfrac{3}{5} \quad \therefore r = 37^\circ \)

**Path length in water.** The refracted ray travels obliquely, so it is *longer* than the depth. If \( d = 36\ \text{cm} \) is the depth, the slant path is
\( s = \dfrac{d}{\cos r} = \dfrac{36}{4/5} = 45\ \text{cm} = 0.45\ \text{m} \)

**Speed in water.**
\( v = \dfrac{c}{n} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{4/3} = 2.25 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s} \)

**Time taken.**
\( t = \dfrac{s}{v} = \dfrac{0.45}{2.25 \times 10^{8}} = 2 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s} \)

\( \therefore t = 2\ \text{ns} \)

*Note the two traps: the light must travel the slant path 45 cm, not the depth 36 cm, and it travels at \( c/n \), not at \( c \). Using 36 cm and \( c \) would give 1.2 ns.*

stem: Estimate the number of images produced if a tiny object is kept in between two plane mirrors inclined at \( 35^{0} \), \( 36^{0} \), \( 40^{0} \) and \( 45^{0} \).
our_solution:
Use the chapter's rule (Table 9.1). Calculate \( n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} \) and let \( N \) be the number of images:
(I) \( n \) an **even integer** \( \Rightarrow N = n - 1 \), wherever the object is;
(II) \( n \) an **odd integer** and object exactly on the angle bisector \( \Rightarrow N = n - 1 \);
(III) \( n \) an **odd integer** and object off the bisector \( \Rightarrow N = n \);
(IV) \( n \) **not an integer** \( \Rightarrow N = m \), the integral part of \( n \).

| \( \theta \) | \( n = \dfrac{360}{\theta} \) | Case | \( N \) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \( 35^\circ \) | \( 10.29 \) | not an integer (IV) | \( 10 \) |
| \( 36^\circ \) | \( 10 \) | even integer (I) | \( 9 \) |
| \( 40^\circ \) | \( 9 \) | odd integer (II)/(III) | \( 8 \) on the bisector, \( 9 \) off it |
| \( 45^\circ \) | \( 8 \) | even integer (I) | \( 7 \) |

\( \therefore \) the numbers of images are **10, 9, (9 or 8) and 7** respectively.

*Only the \( 40^\circ \) case is ambiguous, because 9 is the only odd \( n \) here; for the two even values the position of the object makes no difference at all.*

stem: A rectangular sheet of length 30 cm and breadth 3 cm is kept on the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 30 cm. Draw the image formed by the mirror on the same ray diagram, as far as possible on scale.
book_answer: Inverted image starts from 50 cm and ends at 90 cm. Its height in the beginning is 2 cm and at the end it is 6 cm. At 60 cm, image height is 3 cm. Thus, outer boundary if the image is a curve
our_solution:
**Set-up.** Concave mirror, so \( f = -30\ \text{cm} \). The sheet lies **along** the principal axis, so its two ends are at different object distances and are imaged at different places; its 3 cm breadth is perpendicular to the axis and is magnified by \( |m| = \left| \dfrac{v}{u} \right| \) at each point.

*The stem does not state where along the axis the sheet is placed. To reproduce the printed answer take the 30 cm sheet **centred on the centre of curvature** \( C \) \( (= 2f = 60\ \text{cm}) \), i.e. running from **45 cm to 75 cm** from the pole.*

**Near end, \( u = -45\ \text{cm} \):**
\( \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-45} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{45} = -\dfrac{1}{90} \quad \therefore v = -90\ \text{cm} \)
\( m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-90}{-45} = -2 \quad \therefore \text{height} = 2 \times 3 = 6\ \text{cm} \)

**Far end, \( u = -75\ \text{cm} \):**
\( \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-75} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{75} = -\dfrac{1}{50} \quad \therefore v = -50\ \text{cm} \)
\( m = -\dfrac{-50}{-75} = -\dfrac{2}{3} \quad \therefore \text{height} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 3 = 2\ \text{cm} \)

**Mid point, \( u = -60\ \text{cm} \) (at \( C \)):** \( v = -60\ \text{cm} \), \( m = -1 \), height \( = 3\ \text{cm} \).

**Result.** The image is **real and inverted** (all \( v \) negative, all \( m \) negative), and it **starts at 50 cm and ends at 90 cm** from the pole. Its height is **2 cm at the 50 cm end** and **6 cm at the 90 cm end**, passing through **3 cm at 60 cm**.

**Drawing it.** Mark \( F \) at 30 cm and \( C \) at 60 cm. Draw the object as a thin strip from 45 cm to 75 cm above the axis and its image as a strip from 50 cm to 90 cm below it. Note that the image is 40 cm long where the object was 30 cm, and that the three heights 2, 3, 6 cm do **not** grow uniformly along it: the outer boundary of the image is therefore a **curve**, not a straight line.

stem: A car uses a convex mirror of curvature 1.2 m as its rear-view mirror. A minibus of cross section \( 2.4\ \text{m} \times 2.4\ \text{m} \) is 6.6 m away from the mirror. Estimate the image size.
our_solution:
**Given:** convex mirror, \( R = +1.2\ \text{m} \), so \( f = \dfrac{R}{2} = +0.6\ \text{m} \); object distance \( u = -6.6\ \text{m} \); object a square of side 2.4 m.

**Image distance.**
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{0.6} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-6.6} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{0.6} + \dfrac{1}{6.6} = \dfrac{11 + 1}{6.6} = \dfrac{12}{6.6} \quad \therefore v = 0.55\ \text{m} \)
The positive \( v \) confirms a **virtual image behind the mirror**, as a convex mirror always gives.

**Magnification.**
\( m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{0.55}{-6.6} = +\dfrac{1}{12} = 0.0833 \)
The positive value confirms an **erect** image, and \( m < 1 \) a **diminished** one.

**Image size.** Both dimensions of the cross-section are perpendicular to the axis, so both are scaled by the same \( m \):
\( 2.4 \times \dfrac{1}{12} = 0.2\ \text{m} \)

\( \therefore \) the image is **a square of edge 0.2 m**, erect and virtual.

*This is why a rear-view mirror carries the warning that objects are closer than they appear: a 2.4 m wide minibus only 6.6 m away is shown just 20 cm across.*

stem: A glass slab of thickness 2.5 cm having refractive index 5/3 is kept on an ink spot. A transparent beaker of very thin bottom, containing water of refractive index 4/3 up to 8 cm, is kept on the glass block. Calculate apparent depth of the ink spot when seen from the outside air.
our_solution:
For refraction at a **plane** surface, \( n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}} \), so each layer contributes an apparent depth of \( \dfrac{\text{its real thickness}}{\text{its refractive index}} \). The beaker's bottom is *very thin*, so it adds nothing, and the two layers can simply be added:

**Glass slab:** real thickness 2.5 cm, \( n = \dfrac{5}{3} \)
\( \therefore \) apparent thickness \( = \dfrac{2.5}{5/3} = 2.5 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 1.5\ \text{cm} \)

**Water column:** real thickness 8 cm, \( n = \dfrac{4}{3} \)
\( \therefore \) apparent thickness \( = \dfrac{8}{4/3} = 8 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 6\ \text{cm} \)

**Total apparent depth of the ink spot as seen from the outside air:**
\( = 1.5 + 6 = 7.5\ \text{cm} \)

The real depth is \( 2.5 + 8 = 10.5\ \text{cm} \), so the spot appears raised by 3 cm. Note that each layer must be divided by **its own** refractive index; dividing the total 10.5 cm by either single index would be wrong.

stem: A convex lens held some distance above a 6 cm long pencil produces its image of SOME size. On shifting the lens by a distance equal to its focal length, it again produces the image of the SAME size as earlier. Determine the image size.
our_solution:
For a thin lens, \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} \) and the linear magnification is \( m = \dfrac{v}{u} \). Eliminating \( v \),
\( m = \dfrac{f}{f + u} \)

**The two positions.** The object (the pencil) and the lens are shifted apart by the focal length, so the second object distance is \( u_{2} = u_{1} - f \). The image is of the **same size**, so the two magnifications are equal in magnitude; they cannot be equal in sign, since a lens cannot give the identical magnification at two different object distances. Hence \( m_{2} = -m_{1} \):

\( \dfrac{f}{f + u_{1}} = -\dfrac{f}{f + (u_{1} - f)} = -\dfrac{f}{u_{1}} \)
\( \therefore u_{1} = -(f + u_{1}) \quad \therefore u_{1} = -\dfrac{f}{2} \)

**Magnification.**
\( m_{1} = \dfrac{f}{f - \dfrac{f}{2}} = \dfrac{f}{\dfrac{f}{2}} = +2 \)
and for the second position \( u_{2} = -\dfrac{f}{2} - f = -\dfrac{3f}{2} \), giving
\( m_{2} = \dfrac{f}{f - \dfrac{3f}{2}} = \dfrac{f}{-\dfrac{f}{2}} = -2 \)

So in the first position the object is **within the focus** and the image is virtual, erect and twice the object; in the second it is between \( f \) and \( 2f \) and the image is real, inverted and twice the object. Either way \( |m| = 2 \).

**Image size.**
\( = |m| \times \text{object size} = 2 \times 6 = 12\ \text{cm} \)

stem:
Figure below shows the section ABCD of a transparent slab. There is a tiny green LED light source at the bottom left corner B. A certain ray of light from B suffers total internal reflection at nearest point P on the surface AD and strikes the surface CD at point Q. Determine refractive index of the material of the slab and distance DQ. At Q, the ray PQ will suffer partial or total internal reflection? [You may use the approximation given in Q 1 above].

[Figure: ABCD is a rectangle drawn with A at the top left, D at the top right, B at the bottom left and C at the bottom right. The bottom edge BC measures 6 cm and the right-hand edge from D down to C measures 3 cm. P is marked on the top edge AD with AP = 4 cm, and Q is marked on the right-hand edge DC. The approximation referred to is the one stated in numerical (i) above: the angles of the 3:4:5 Pythagorean triangle are nearly \( 37^{0} \), \( 53^{0} \) and \( 90^{0} \).]
book_answer: n = 5/4, DQ = 1.5 cm, Partial internal reflection at Q
our_solution:
Take \( B \) as the origin, with \( BC \) along the \( x \)-axis. From the figure, \( B = (0, 0) \), \( C = (6, 0) \), \( D = (6, 3) \), \( A = (0, 3) \) (in cm), and \( P = (4, 3) \) on \( AD \).

**Refractive index.** The ray \( BP \) has horizontal and vertical projections 4 cm and 3 cm, so \( BP = \sqrt{4^{2} + 3^{2}} = 5\ \text{cm} \) — the 3:4:5 triangle of numerical (i). The normal at the surface \( AD \) is vertical, so the angle of incidence at \( P \) satisfies
\( \sin i = \dfrac{4}{5} \quad \therefore i = 53^\circ \)
The stem says \( P \) is the **nearest** point on \( AD \) at which total internal reflection occurs. A point nearer to \( A \) would be reached by a ray of *smaller* angle of incidence, so \( P \) is exactly the borderline case and this angle is the **critical angle**:
\( \sin(i_{c}) = \dfrac{4}{5} \quad \therefore n = \dfrac{1}{\sin(i_{c})} = \dfrac{5}{4} = 1.25 \)

**Distance DQ.** At \( P \) the ray reflects off the horizontal surface \( AD \), so its vertical component reverses while the horizontal one is unchanged: the direction \( (4, 3) \) becomes \( (4, -3) \). Travelling from \( P = (4, 3) \) it reaches the surface \( CD \) at \( x = 6 \), i.e. after a horizontal run of 2 cm, so it drops \( 2 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 1.5\ \text{cm} \).
\( \therefore Q = (6,\ 1.5) \quad \text{and} \quad DQ = 3 - 1.5 = 1.5\ \text{cm} \)

**What happens at Q.** The surface \( CD \) is vertical, so its normal is **horizontal**. The ray \( PQ \) has direction \( (4, -3) \), so the angle it makes with that horizontal normal satisfies
\( \sin i' = \dfrac{3}{5} \quad \therefore i' = 37^\circ \)
Since \( 37^\circ < i_{c} = 53^\circ \), the condition for total internal reflection is **not** met at \( Q \).

\( \therefore \) at \( Q \) the ray suffers only **partial internal reflection** — most of the light refracts out of the slab there.

**Answers:** \( n = \dfrac{5}{4} \), \( DQ = 1.5\ \text{cm} \), partial internal reflection at \( Q \).

*The key point is that the two surfaces are perpendicular, so an angle of \( 53^\circ \) from the normal at \( AD \) is an angle of \( 37^\circ \) from the normal at \( CD \); the same ray is above the critical angle at one face and below it at the other.*

stem:
A point object is kept 10 cm away from one of the surfaces of a thick double convex lens of refractive index 1.5 and radii of curvature 10 cm and 8 cm. Central thickness of the lens is 2 cm. Determine location of the final image considering paraxial rays only.
**Hint :** Single spherical surface formula to be used twice.
book_answer: 64 cm away from the other surface
our_solution:
The lens is **thick**, so the thin-lens (lens makers') formula cannot be used. As the hint says, apply the single-spherical-surface relation
\( \dfrac{n_{2} - n_{1}}{R} = \dfrac{n_{2}}{v} - \dfrac{n_{1}}{u} \)
twice, remembering that \( n_{1} \) is always the refractive index of the medium of the **real object** for that surface.

**First surface** \( (R_{1} = +10\ \text{cm} \), double convex, facing the object).
\( n_{1} = 1 \), \( n_{2} = 1.5 \), \( u = -10\ \text{cm} \):
\( \dfrac{1.5 - 1}{+10} = \dfrac{1.5}{v_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{-10} \)
\( \therefore 0.05 = \dfrac{1.5}{v_{1}} + 0.1 \quad \therefore \dfrac{1.5}{v_{1}} = -0.05 \quad \therefore v_{1} = -30\ \text{cm} \)
The negative sign means the first surface alone would form a **virtual** image 30 cm on the object's side of it.

**Second surface** \( (R_{2} = -8\ \text{cm}) \). This virtual image is the object for the second surface, which is 2 cm further along, so
\( u = -30 - 2 = -32\ \text{cm} \)
Now the incident rays are inside the glass, so \( n_{1} = 1.5 \) and \( n_{2} = 1 \):
\( \dfrac{1 - 1.5}{-8} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1.5}{-32} \)
\( \therefore 0.0625 = \dfrac{1}{v} + 0.046875 \quad \therefore \dfrac{1}{v} = 0.015625 \quad \therefore v = +64\ \text{cm} \)

\( \therefore \) the final image is real and lies **64 cm away from the other (second) surface** of the lens.

*Two places where sign care matters: the intermediate image distance must have the central thickness 2 cm subtracted (not added) to give the object distance for the second surface, and \( n_{1} \) and \( n_{2} \) swap over between the two surfaces.*

stem: A monochromatic ray of light is incident at \( 37^{0} \) on an equilateral prism of refractive index 3/2. Determine angle of emergence and angle of deviation. If angle of prism is adjustable, what should its value be for emergent ray to be just possible for the same angle of incidence.
book_answer: e = 63°, δ = 40°, A = 65° 24' for e = 90° (just emerges)
our_solution:
**Given:** equilateral prism, so \( A = 60^\circ \); \( n = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5 \); \( i = 37^\circ \), for which \( \sin 37^\circ = 0.6 \).

**First refraction.**
\( \sin r_{1} = \dfrac{\sin i}{n} = \dfrac{0.6}{1.5} = 0.4 \quad \therefore r_{1} = 23^\circ 35' \)

**Second refraction.** For a prism, \( r_{1} + r_{2} = A \):
\( r_{2} = 60^\circ - 23^\circ 35' = 36^\circ 25' \)
\( \sin e = n \sin r_{2} = 1.5 \times 0.5937 = 0.8906 \quad \therefore e \cong 63^\circ \)

**Angle of deviation.** \( i + e = A + \delta \):
\( \delta = i + e - A = 37^\circ + 63^\circ - 60^\circ = 40^\circ \)

**Largest prism angle for which the ray still emerges.** The emergent ray just fails to appear when \( e = 90^\circ \), i.e. when \( r_{2} \) equals the critical angle. For \( n = 1.5 \),
\( \sin(i_{c}) = \dfrac{1}{1.5} \quad \therefore i_{c} = 41^\circ 49' \)
The angle of incidence is unchanged, so \( r_{1} \) is still \( 23^\circ 35' \), and since \( A = r_{1} + r_{2} \),
\( A_{max} = 23^\circ 35' + 41^\circ 49' = 65^\circ 24' \)

**Answers:** \( e = 63^\circ \), \( \delta = 40^\circ \), and \( A = 65^\circ 24' \) for the emergent ray to be just possible \( (e = 90^\circ \), the ray just grazes out).

*For any prism angle larger than \( 65^\circ 24' \), \( r_{2} \) would exceed the critical angle and the ray would be totally internally reflected inside the prism instead of emerging.*

stem: From the given data set, determine angular dispersion by the prism and dispersive power of its material for extreme colours. \( n_{R} = 1.62 \), \( n_{V} = 1.66 \), \( \delta_{R} = 3.1^\circ \)
our_solution:
**Given:** \( n_{R} = 1.62 \), \( n_{V} = 1.66 \), \( \delta_{R} = 3.1^\circ \). Nothing is said about the refracting angle, so first recover it.

**Refracting angle.** For a thin prism \( \delta = A(n - 1) \), so
\( A = \dfrac{\delta_{R}}{n_{R} - 1} = \dfrac{3.1}{1.62 - 1} = \dfrac{3.1}{0.62} = 5^\circ \)

**Deviation of violet.**
\( \delta_{V} = A(n_{V} - 1) = 5(1.66 - 1) = 5 \times 0.66 = 3.3^\circ \)

**Angular dispersion.**
\( \delta_{VR} = \delta_{V} - \delta_{R} = 3.3 - 3.1 = 0.2^\circ \)
(Equivalently, directly: \( \delta_{VR} = A(n_{V} - n_{R}) = 5 \times 0.04 = 0.2^\circ \).)

**Dispersive power.** With yellow as the mean colour, \( n_{Y} = \dfrac{n_{V} + n_{R}}{2} = \dfrac{1.66 + 1.62}{2} = 1.64 \):
\( \omega_{VR} = \dfrac{n_{V} - n_{R}}{n_{Y} - 1} = \dfrac{0.04}{0.64} = \dfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625 \)

(The same value follows from the deviations: \( \omega = \dfrac{\delta_{V} - \delta_{R}}{\left( \dfrac{\delta_{V} + \delta_{R}}{2} \right)} = \dfrac{0.2}{3.2} = \dfrac{1}{16} \).)

**Answers:** \( \delta_{VR} = 0.2^\circ \), \( \omega_{VR} = \dfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625 \).

*Note that \( \omega \) does not need \( A \) at all — the refracting angle cancels, which is why dispersive power is a property of the material only. This value is about twice that of an ordinary crown glass \( (\approx 0.03) \).*

stem: Refractive index of a flint glass varies from 1.60 to 1.66 for visible range. Radii of curvature of a thin convex lens are 10 cm and 15 cm. Calculate the chromatic aberration between extreme colours.
our_solution:
For a **thin convex** lens the two radii are of opposite sign; taking \( R_{1} = +10\ \text{cm} \) and \( R_{2} = -15\ \text{cm} \),
\( K = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{-15} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{3 + 2}{30} = \dfrac{1}{6}\ \text{cm}^{-1} \)

The extreme colours are red \( (n_{R} = 1.60 \), the smallest index, so the least deviated) and violet \( (n_{V} = 1.66) \).

**Focal length for red.**
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{R}} = (n_{R} - 1)K = (1.60 - 1) \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{0.6}{6} = 0.1 \quad \therefore f_{R} = 10\ \text{cm} \)

**Focal length for violet.**
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{V}} = (n_{V} - 1)K = (1.66 - 1) \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{0.66}{6} = 0.11 \quad \therefore f_{V} = \dfrac{100}{11}\ \text{cm} = 9.09\ \text{cm} \)

**Longitudinal chromatic aberration** (the separation of the two foci):
\( f_{R} - f_{V} = 10 - \dfrac{100}{11} = \dfrac{110 - 100}{11} = \dfrac{10}{11}\ \text{cm} \cong 0.91\ \text{cm} \)

\( \therefore \) the chromatic aberration between the extreme colours is \( \dfrac{10}{11}\ \text{cm} \).

*Violet has the larger refractive index, hence the larger deviation and the **shorter** focal length — it is focused closest to the pole, exactly as the chapter states.*

stem: A person uses spectacles of 'number' 2.00 for reading. Determine the range of magnifying power (angular magnification) possible. It is a concavo-convex lens \( (n = 1.5) \) having curvature of one of its surfaces to be 10 cm. Estimate that of the other.
our_solution:
**Range of magnifying power.** The 'number' of the spectacles is the focal power in dioptre, so
\( P = +2.00\ \text{D} \quad \therefore f = \dfrac{1}{P} = 0.5\ \text{m} = 50\ \text{cm} \)
Used for reading, the lens is a simple microscope, whose magnifying power lies between \( \dfrac{D}{f} \) and \( 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \). With \( D = 25\ \text{cm} \):
\( M_{min} = \dfrac{D}{f} = \dfrac{25}{50} = 0.5 \)
\( M_{max} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 \)
So the angular magnification ranges from **0.5 to 1.5**. (A focal length as long as 50 cm gives very little magnification; these spectacles correct the eye's focusing rather than magnify.)

**The other radius of curvature.** For a **concavo-convex** (meniscus) lens both centres of curvature lie on the same side, so — as in the chapter's cataract-spectacle example — both radii carry the **same sign**; take them positive, with the convex face receiving the incident rays. Let \( R_{1} = +10\ \text{cm} \), \( n = 1.5 \), \( f = +50\ \text{cm} \).

\( \dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{50} = (1.5 - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \right) \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{5 - 2}{50} = \dfrac{3}{50} \)
\( \therefore R_{2} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{cm} \cong 16.7\ \text{cm} \)

**Answers:** \( M_{min} = 0.5 \), \( M_{max} = 1.5 \), \( R_{2} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{cm} \).

*Both radii come out positive and unequal, which is exactly what a meniscus of positive focal length requires: the surface facing the object must be the more strongly curved one.*

stem: Focal power of the eye lens of a compound microscope is 6 dioptre. The microscope is to be used for maximum magnifying power (angular magnification) of at least 12.5. The packing instructions demand that length of the microscope should be 25 cm. Determine minimum focal power of the objective. How much will its radius of curvature be if it is a biconvex lens of \( n = 1.5 \).
our_solution:
**Given:** \( P_{e} = 6\ \text{D} \), so \( f_{e} = \dfrac{100}{6} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{cm} \); required \( M \geq 12.5 \); length \( L = 25\ \text{cm} \); \( D = 25\ \text{cm} \).

**Eye lens.** Maximum magnifying power means the final image is at \( D \), so
\( M_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} = 1 + \dfrac{25}{50/3} = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 \)

**Required magnification of the objective.** \( M = m_{o} \times M_{e} \):
\( m_{o} = \dfrac{M}{M_{e}} = \dfrac{12.5}{2.5} = 5 \)

**Position of the intermediate image.** For the eye lens, \( v_{e} = -25\ \text{cm} \):
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{v_{e}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} \quad \therefore \dfrac{3}{50} = \dfrac{1}{-25} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} = -\dfrac{1}{25} - \dfrac{3}{50} = -\dfrac{2 + 3}{50} = -\dfrac{1}{10} \quad \therefore |u_{e}| = 10\ \text{cm} \)

**Objective.** The length is the separation of the lenses, \( L = |v_{o}| + |u_{e}| \):
\( |v_{o}| = 25 - 10 = 15\ \text{cm} \)
and from \( m_{o} = \dfrac{|v_{o}|}{|u_{o}|} \),
\( |u_{o}| = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore \dfrac{1}{f_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{v_{o}} - \dfrac{1}{u_{o}} = \dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1 + 5}{15} = \dfrac{2}{5} \quad \therefore f_{o} = 2.5\ \text{cm} \)
\( \therefore P_{o} = \dfrac{100}{f_{o}\ (\text{cm})} = \dfrac{100}{2.5} = 40\ \text{D} \)

This is the **minimum** focal power: a smaller \( P_{o} \) means a larger \( f_{o} \) and hence a smaller \( m_{o} \), which would push \( M \) below 12.5.

**Radius of curvature.** For a thin symmetric **biconvex** lens, \( R_{1} = +R \) and \( R_{2} = -R \), so
\( \dfrac{1}{f_{o}} = (n - 1)\left( \dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{-R} \right) = \dfrac{2(n - 1)}{R} \)
\( \therefore R = 2(n - 1)f_{o} = 2(1.5 - 1)(2.5) = 2.5\ \text{cm} \)
(the familiar result that for \( n = 1.5 \) a symmetric biconvex lens has \( f = R \)).

**Answers:** minimum focal power of the objective \( = 40\ \text{dioptre} \); radius of curvature \( = 2.5\ \text{cm} \).
